speechtext:
What is the total amount of revenue collected from income tax paid on pension income by taxpayers for (a) 1973 (b) 1974 (c) 1975?
Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Finance): Under the Canadian income tax system, tax is levied on the composite of income from all sources and not on individual components. Thus, conceptually, it is not possible to precisely determine the tax revenues associated with any individual income component. Under the Income Tax Act, tax is levied on four distinct types of pension income. These include payments under the Old Age Security Act, benefits under the Canada/Quebec Pension Plan, private pension income from registered pension plans and distributions from registered retirement savings plans, either in lump sums (subject to income averaging provisions) or as annuity income. In addition, all pension income received by the dependent spouse of a taxpayer served to reduce the marital exemption claimable in respect of that spouse in the 1973 and 1974 taxation years. The amount of this pension income is not reported separately on the income tax form and thus is not separately identified in income tax statistics. Estimates of the revenue consequences of the taxation of all types of pension income would require special data processing, the costs of which would be several thousands of dollars. Furthermore, a complete accounting of the revenue consequences of the taxation of certain types of pension income would require an accounting of the fact that employer and employee contributions to the Canada/Quebec Pension Plans and to private pension plans are deductible from income in computing tax.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (for the Minister of Agriculture) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING ADVANCE PAYMENTS FOR CROPS
speechtext: that Bill C-2, to facilitate the making of advance payments for crops, be read the third time and do pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING ADVANCE PAYMENTS FOR CROPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no quarrel with the principle and objective of Bill C-2. The quarrel is with the method of implementation and the lack of availability of this program to all farmers who are producing storable crops. There is precedent for a different structure other than the one proposed. For instance, in the Wheat Board the only security that is required for a grain producer is that he sign his permit book and place his crop virtually at the disposal of the Wheat Board as they advance him cash, under the advance payments program on the government. It is simple; it is workable; it is safe.
There are other programs in government which could operate on a very simple basis. In the case of farm improvement loans it is negotiation between the applicant and his bank, his financial institution, his co-operative or his caisse populaire. This would provide a reasonable approach for farmers to the funds which the government is making available for this purpose. It is customary for legislation in this country, and the regulations associated with it, to be presented in rather convoluted language, establishing a difficult method of procedure in order that moneys may be spent. There is no necessity for it in this structure.
It would be advisable for the Minister of Agriculture and the government to examine the method used in the United States for comparable purposes. If a person requires an advance payment or a loan on grain stored, in the United States the applicant simply goes to the financial institution of his choice, presents his credentials, describes his inventory, describes his storage capability and, if necessary, passes over the key to the financial institution which makes the loan. The government of the United States is the guarantor of the loan; the bank has no chance of loss. The farmer has the money which he requires.
1 see no reason why we in Canada should complicate the program for advance payments on crops, as we are at present. In many instances there is no organization in place to act as the instrument of the government of Canada or the Minister of Agriculture. In many instances farmers do not wish to belong to organizations. Both these groups are prohibited from participating in this program. In addition to that, the minister has laid down qualifications respecting whether an organization is or is not eligible. To complicate it even further, organizations of Canadian farmers have suggested that under the present obscure proposal they do not know whether they wish to act, under this act, as bankers for the minister and the government.

It was moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) that we should extend borrowing privileges to farmers by means of their financial institutions. This is a very logical, proper, feasible and easy fashion in which farmers might obtain this money. I supported that amendment, and continue to do so. I think it would do for the financial institutions what the government cannot do. Perhaps I should say that the financial institutions can do better what the government tries to do. For instance, financial institutions such as banks would have a very easy opportunity to check the inventory, the quality of storage and the qualifications of the applicant. I think financial institutions ought to earn their interest by providing guaranteed loans in accordance with the government's legislation.
Experience shows that losses sustained under guaranteed farm improvement loan legislation have been negligible. That shows how well the farm improvement loan legislation is administered. The government guarantees a portion of the loan. The financial institution lends money to the applicant and does its best to ensure that the applicant uses equipment properly and makes regular payments. Therefore, on behalf of the government the lender performs a service for the farmer and in the process earns interest. I think what has worked in connection with the farm improvement loans structure would also work in connection with this bill. I have received inquiries from people interested in obtaining such loans.
Since the government has rejected an amendment to allow banks to be the government's agent rather than organizations, and since it is intended to extend the provisions of the bill to farm groups, perhaps provincial ministers of agriculture could be persuaded to act as the delegated instruments of the federal Minister of Agriculture in the implementation of this process. That is a second alternative. Perhaps the government could adopt it in order to make the scheme workable, available to farmers, and to make it democratic, not autocratic. The bill orders farmers to join. It virtually compels certain organizations to participate in the program. I suggest the government is abdicating its responsibility with respect to all citizens of Canada by enacting such legislation. This is a wrong move.
There is no use belabouring the point. I hope, since this bill is to be considered in the other place, that the government will reconsider its adamant position. Let it make the provisions of the bill available to all farmers, and let it allow loans to be available in the way farm improvement loans are available from banks or other financial institutions. In addition, I suggest that the federal Minister of Agriculture should make arrangements whereby his provincial counterparts will act as agents and assume responsibility on behalf of farmers. I submit that this piece of legislation is intended to attain the philosophical ends of the minister, rather than a solution to the problems of farmers mentioned earlier in this debate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING ADVANCE PAYMENTS FOR CROPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at length but I wish to bring forward a few points because I am disturbed by certain developments con-
April 1, 1977

cerning the income of western farmers and farmers all across Canada.
I agree with the principle of extending cash advances. Farmers want, and need, this type of legislation. Many in this country are under the mistaken impression that farmers these days are doing well. True, grain in the last few years has fetched high prices. Between $4 and $5 per bushel has been charged, and some time ago prices were in the $6 range. People who watched the CBC program "Our Breadbasket", a program which dealt with two farmers, one owning an airplane and the other a swimming pool, might be under the impression that all farmers are doing very well. That is wrong, and we must make sure consumers in this country are not left with that impression. The consumers of this country have a soft spot for farmers and understand their problems. Farmers appreciate the concern of consumers. Unfortunately, the sort of distortions of the truth one sees, for example, on television programs, leaves consumers with the wrong impression; good relations between farmers and consumers may degenerate and we may run into difficulties in food production.
According to a Statistics Canada report issued three weeks ago-this is of concern to the acting minister of agriculture who comes from Quebec-gross farm income in Canada, January over January 1976 to 1977, declined by 31 per cent. Farm income in the four western provinces from January, 1976, to January, 1977, declined by 38 per cent. That is why a bill providing for cash advance to farmers is important. Of course, it only provides a cash advance on the crops they sell. The fact is, as 1 have said, that farm incomes in this country are dropping rapidly. The House ought to be aware of this fact, because we should do our best to pass legislation which will give farmers security of income. Cash advances are only a picayune part of any program which will guarantee the farmer a decent livelihood. After all, it is only an advance on what the farmer will realize later from his sales. The farmer needs the sort of income security which many in this country enjoy. Sometimes income security is not great, especially for the unemployed. Unfortunately, at present the farmer does not have security of income. He needs it, especially at this time when farm incomes in the country are falling rapidly.
Many do not realize that although a farmer's income may fall, his input costs remain the same or may even rise. Farm machinery prices are outrageously high. International Harvester, Massey-Ferguson and other farm machinery manufacturers have maintained farm machinery prices at a high level. They took advantage a few years ago of high grain prices, raised their machinery prices and have kept those prices high. If this situation continues you will see huge lay-offs of farm machinery workers in places like Brantford because farmers will not be able to afford farm machinery. As a result, more Canadians will lose their jobs.
We ought to consider a farmer's input costs when debating a bill affecting farm income. It is important to guarantee the farmer's income but it is equally important to guarantee orderly marketing. Farmers need marketing boards and marketing agencies to bargain on their behalf in the marketplace.

Such boards and agencies give them a clout and help them even out the peaks and valleys of prices paid under our so-called free market system. Thus it can be assured to some extent that farmers will obtain at least a minimum reasonable price for their commodities. That system is also good for the consumer because he will not be at the mercy of the forces of supply and demand to such a great extent when buying his bacon at the corner grocery store or the other commodities which he needs. In addition, we must guarantee a minimum price for farm commodities in this country and make sure that we maintain controls over the price of commodities which farmers use, such as machinery and fertilizer.
Let me mention something else which has concerned me for a long time. I mention it now because the point is raised in the "bible" of the House of Commons, the Globe and Mail. A story on the front page of our "bible" says that people who buy cheaper foreign foods are undermining our farmers. So charges the minister of agriculture of the province of Ontario. That point is worth noting. I do not think we should build great tariff walls inhibiting trade between this country and other countries. I do not favour a great deal of protectionism in this country or elsewhere. I like to see as much free trade as possible, a world community the members of which help one another, a community which genuinely tries to redistribute wealth and income. I am speaking of redistribution not merely within countries but between countries, between the more prosperous parts of the world and the developing world.
On the other hand, the point must be made, when one talks about this country's tariff structure, that the least protected sector of our economy is the farm sector. The average tariff for farm goods in this country is one-half of one per cent; that is all the protection afforded our farmers. Compare this protection with that given the textile industry and the manufacturing industry, particularly of southern Ontario. Compare it with almost any other industry in this country, and you will find that the farmer is getting less protection. Some people are getting tariff protection at the rate of 10 per cent, 20 per cent or more, but the farmer is not. As a result, we Canadians will never become self-sufficient in food 10, 20 or 30 years from now. The Science Council has warned us that by the year 2000, Canada, with its vast acreage, will not be able to feed itself. We will be net importers of food. One of the many reasons for that is the stupidity of governments over the years in not establishing a decent trade and tariff policy for Canada.
There are many examples one could give of our goods competing in other parts of the world. The European Common Market is a good example where tariff barriers are put up by the EEC or other countries. Yet the goods from those countries, which are really subsidized and are helped by support prices, come to our country without any tariff barriers. It seems to me to be a blatant form of discrimination. An example is given in today's Globe and Mail which is probably as good as any in making the point. It is with regard to the food and vegetable market. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said a short time ago that Ontario peach growers had

Australian peaches come into Canada with a tariff of W2 pence per pound, and Australian pears come into Canada duty free. As a result, the share of the market of Ontario peach growers has gone down from 80 per cent to 20 per cent. I predict that if this continues in a short time we will have no Ontario peach producers, or perhaps a few guys here or there, but no significant number of Ontario peach producers and we will be at the whim and mercy of the importers and the peach growers in other countries. Once they have us by the short hairs, they will dictate prices that our consumers will have to pay.
These are the questions that the House should debate some time. These are the questions we will have to resolve if we want a food and agricultural policy in this country which will bring self-sufficiency and security of supply of food for Canadian consumers. At the same time, when we. secure that supply for Canadian consumers we will ensure a secure, decent and adequate income for the food producers of Canada.
I wanted to make those few points this morning before the minister replied to me. There are many other things one could say about farm products in this part of the country. I think of industrial and fluid milk producers and the vast imports of cheese from other parts of the world. I think of the lack of imagination that our governments have displayed in helping our farmers to produce cheese and helping provide jobs for our own people and incomes for our farmers. Then I think of something I discovered only four weeks ago. There are companies in the United States which are producing artificial cheese made of vegetable oils. They inject this cheese with artificial flavouring to make it taste like Cheddar or any other cheese, and also they inject the cheese with artificial colouring to make it look like Cheddar or any other cheese. Then they sell it on the Canadian market. There is a company in Texas which is now lobbying three government departments for the sale of synthetic cheese in Canada which would sell at about two-thirds of the price of real cheese.
Most probably, it does not have anywhere near the same nutritional value and in many ways it would be fraudulent to sell this cheese because people would think they were eating real cheese, instead of which they are eating vegetable oils with different additives. As well, it would undermine the income of farmers. These are genuine threats to farmers' income, and if we do not come up with a comprehensive agricultural policy, then before we are much older we might not be able to produce enough food to feed ourselves. That is a real crime in a country as vast as ours, in a country with so many acres of land and as much potential as we have in Canada. We think of ourselves as a vast food basket, but we are not. We are putting land out of production, according to the Department of Agriculture, at the rate of 250 acres per day, or 10 acres an hour. If that continues, along with the other stupid policies we have we will not be able to feed ourselves and we will become a net importer of food. We will
[Mr. Nystrom.J
have an availability and supply problem which will affect the price of food, and we will have to solve these problems.
We should have in this country a much better co-ordinated food and agricultural policy. At the moment food and agriculture are divided among five or six ministers: the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Transport who is responsible for the Wheat Board, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion who looks after community pastures and other aspects of farming, the Minister of National Health and Welfare who is responsible for the health protection branch and many aspects of nutrition, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who looks after many aspects of pricing, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who deals with tariff and trade policies, and probably two or three other ministers.
I suggest that we combine all these aspects of food and agriculture under one minister, but certainly not many more than one, and come up with a food and agricultural policy which will give us a guaranteed food supply for the consumers and at the same time a secure income for the producers, namely, the farmers. I realize there are a few trade-offs. There has to be some give and take on both sides. But I think we have a feeling in this country that we would be able to accomplish that if we had leadership to take us in that direction as its objective.
The bill before us is only a tiny bill, a bill which most farmers will appreciate, but it is so small it is almost irrelevant in the total scheme of things. What we need is a decent and forward-looking food and agricultural policy for all of us and for our children in the future.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING ADVANCE PAYMENTS FOR CROPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have been impressed with the consistency of the government in doing things in one way if they cannot do it in another. Parts of this bill seem to fall into that category. For years the government has tried to persuade oilseed producing farmers to agree to having their products designated under the Wheat Board, particularly rapeseed and mustard seed, but they have been unable to do so. So now they are providing some protection to those farmers, under Bill C-2, that they were unable to provide in a more direct way. I certainly commend them for their ability to accomplish by a roundabout method what they could not do either directly with the support of the farmers or in any other way.
The previous speaker mentioned what is probably the major problem facing agriculture today. It is highlighted not only by the government's inability to relate the national requirements of Canada to the ability of other countries such as Mexico and the U.S. to dump their surplus vegetables and fruit crops in Canada at a time when our prime crop is coming on the market, thus making it almost impossible to sell Canadian fruits and vegetables where they can be sold at the lowest cost, particularly in areas such as the Niagara peninsula, but its inability to provide Canadians with the same kind of protection that any other area would have when the main portion of their crop comes on the market free of tariff from other countries. This is not possible in Canada. The Ontario minister of agriculture has been screaming loudly about the inability of
April 1, 1977

Ontario farmers to produce and market their products at reasonable prices, not the surplus price but the normal production price which has to compete with U.S. surplus production. The Ontario farmer is really getting the short end of the stick.
To some extent this bill would assist the farmer of Ontario. It would allow him to retain his crop for a period of time, to develop his market and to maximize the price for his commodity. However, it would only do that if we stopped the Americans flooding our market at the time our crops are on the market. In this bill we are applying the same type of legislation we used for cereal grains to fruit and vegetables. They do not fall into the same category. It is quite true that farmers can get advance payments for wheat. They can hold that wheat for two or three years until the market improves, and get a better price, but with fruit and vegetables there is a limit. In some cases that limit is quite short and these commodities cannot be held until there is a better market. Therefore, in allowing each producer a maximum of $15,000 we can expect banks or other financial institutions to advance that money to hold products only if those products can be held and will not deteriorate.
Some potatoes which were sent to Haiti went by slow boat, taking four or five months to get there, and when they got there they were of no value. In fact, it cost a lot of money to clean up the ship.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING ADVANCE PAYMENTS FOR CROPS
speechtext: You need more information on that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING ADVANCE PAYMENTS FOR CROPS
speechtext:
The only information I am presenting is the fact that it did not matter what price those potatoes brought. When they got there, they could not be sold at any price. So if we are going to maximize the price in the market, and if we are going to do it by allowing an advance payment, obviously we are also going to have to do it within the confines of our ability to hold commodities long enough to maximize the price. Many products cannot be held as long as wheat can be held.
Farmers in this country have an organization problem. Farmers want the government to give them subsidies, but they do not want to be organized or restricted. They do not want marketing boards. They do not want to come under quota restrictions. They are really asking for a free market, which means an open border. However, at the same time they know perfectly well that they cannot exist without certain conditions. A number of organizations came before the committee, but there was only one organization prepared to take an administrative role. The bill provides a very small amount for administration. Certain conditions must be met. There have to be audits and financial controls, for which most organizations are not prepared. They have not had to carry out these functions previously and they are not capable of setting up that kind of machinery. There was, however, one organization from Ontario which came forward and said it was in a position to do that and it would be prepared to do it. It is also true that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said it probably had the machinery and the wherewithal, and that if an organization
Advance Payments for Crops
came forward and wanted to take advantage of cash advances for a specific commodity, that kind of machinery could be provided. However, that federation was not asked to do that.
We will have to face the fact that if farmers are going to be guaranteed prices, that will have to be done in an orderly way and there will have to be orderly marketing. Producers will have to submit to some types of control because with most commodities the import-export market will have to be controlled. Import bans will have to be put on certain commodities so that the market will not be unfairly flooded. There will have to be control of the export market, because if prices go up in another country it is possible for a selfish group of producers to send that commodity out of the country, leaving it unavailable to consumers in Canada. Orderly marketing would provide commodities to consumers at reasonable prices, and a reasonable return for producers.
Very shortly the government will have to consider some method of providing the almost immediate imposition of tariffs or outright bans against the importation of goods during specific seasons. Let us consider tomatoes, for example. When our tomatoes come on the market, that is when there is a surplus of tomatoes in the United States. The United States crop year is finished and there is a surplus there. American tomatoes come into Canada at the same price they are sold in the United States. This does not really defeat GATT, but as far as our producers are concerned those tomatoes are being dumped into Canada at far below the cost of production of our crops. Our crops compete with the United States surplus. There should be a ban on the importation of that surplus for the benefit of our producers, our producer organizations, our agricultural agencies and, indeed, our provincial ministers of agriculture.
The Ontario minister of agriculture said that it would be very nice if the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce responded to his demand for restrictions on some commodities. He made an application in 1973 and has heard nothing as yet. It is possible that some commodities like wheat may be kept for years, but I think there would be difficulty with some other commodities.
Unless someone else wishes to speak, in one moment I am going to resume my seat so that this bill can be passed.

speechtext:
That in accordance with section 19 of an act respecting the status of the official languages of Canada, chapter 0-2, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970, this House approves the reappointment of Keith Spicer, Esquire, as Commissioner of Official Languages of Canada, for a term expiring July 31, 1977.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my comments will be very brief indeed. The commissioner has completed a full term in this post, and on behalf of all members of the House, I am sure, I want to express to him our appreciation of his dedication and the contribution he has made to the country.

subsubtopic: REAPPOINTMENT OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REAPPOINTMENT OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I am sure other hon. members will want to make the same point in their comments, because I believe it is universally shared. The purpose of this motion is to extend the term for an additional four months. Before that period expires, of course, it will be necessary to bring before the House a motion to provide for a successor to the present commissioner for a full term. Because that motion will have to come forward before the end of this present session, it would provide an opportunity for hon. members to discuss the issues of substance that may arise in connection with the new appointment.
There is some urgency to passing this motion today because the term expired last evening. It is desirable to maintain the continuity of the office by passing this motion. In asking the House to deal with it expeditiously, I hold out the assurance that it will be possible for hon. members, before the end of this session, under another motion to discuss at greater length matters that may interest them.

subsubtopic: REAPPOINTMENT OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before speaking directly to this motion I feel compelled to make two or three comments. My first is to join the government House leader in complimenting the Commissioner of Official Languages on his frankness, straightforwardness and ability to speak out clearly when criticism is deserved. My
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
second refers to a procedural matter related to the manner in which this motion was first presented to us.
My understanding is that the government House leader secured an undertaking from the opposition parties to accept this motion without debate. This undertaking was obtained before the commissioner's report was tabled with, one is tempted to believe, the hope that the report of the language commissioner would pass without comment. The government obviously was aware of the nature of the comments in the commissioner's report, and therefore obtained this undertaking with knowledge of facts which were not at that time revealed to the opposition.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REAPPOINTMENT OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because it is an important matter 1 would like to assure the hon. member that when the request was made it was not made known to me that the report was to be tabled at this particular time. In fact, I realized the moment the report was tabled, which was an action taken independently, that it would create difficulties in having the motion passed without debate. It was quite unknown to me that this tabling would take place at the time it did.

subsubtopic: REAPPOINTMENT OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am obliged, in view of parliamentary practice, to accept the explanation given by the government House leader. I will, therefore, withhold any further comments which were in a way a stricture of the government for having tried something and not having succeeded in doing it. I will leave that aside. [Translation]
There are more preliminary comments. First of all, I wish to indicate unequivocally that the Progressive Conservative Party fully and unreservedly supports the Official Languages Act and acknowledges to Canadians, first the right to deal with the federal government in the language of their choice, and second the right to integrate with the federal administration with the assurance that they will be able to work in one or the other of our official languages in the sectors of this administration which are designated bilingual or unilingual. That, Mr. Speaker, is the nature of our commitment towards the Official Languages Act, a commitment which cannot be questioned. [English]
I will now turn to some of the commentaries in the report of the languages commissioner. This will explain the reasons for the support which we propose to give this motion. I wish to cite, first, an article in the Globe and Mail of last Tuesday. This is a report on discussion with the Commissioner of Official Languages. The comment in the Globe and Mail is as follows:
Responsibility for language policy is scattered among five government departments and agencies.
It is well known that there is a disparate responsibility within the government. It falls in many quarters. Mr. Spicer is quoted as saying, and this is a direct quote:
"Plainly, the government cannot pull its information act together until it pulls its administrative act together."
April 1, 1977

In other words, until it decides where the responsibility lies. He went on to say:
"None of this would require genius, or even that favourite government substitute for genius, bloated budgets. Just a sense of what is clear, practical and engaging.
And none of it would do the slightest good without a key ingredient: the political will to explain".

In his report, Mr. Speaker, the commissioner says with the same clearness and openness, and I quote:
Whatever miracles the government may work in adjusting its priorities and administrative plumbing, it shows every sign-nearly eight years after the act's passage-of continuing to sabotage its best efforts through bankrupt information programmes.
If it persists in ignoring the people's need to believe, or even to understand, the government's reckless squandering of goodwill may sooner or later cost our language reform its vital, and newly fragile, popular support.
The commissioner goes on, as reported on page 28:
If the government persists in viewing communication of its purposes, plans and acts as of marginal importance-
I emphasize the word "marginal".
the linguistic cause it must anguish over, still again, will end by striking many as of marginal value, if not of unacceptable annoyance. Surely the passionate events of the past year have told the government that much.
Of course, he is talking about events which took place in another province. I go on quoting:
And warned it that, however sound its reshaping of priorities and methods, if the people know nothing, they will believe nothing. And anything.

That is a sad commentary. Here he brings the matter very close to home. The languages commissioner, in a quotation cited in the Globe and Mail of the same day, picks up the same story and says:
"But in selling bilingualism, particularly in western Canada, the federal government has utterly failed.
I lay the alienation of the language question in the west squarely at the government's doorstep."
By its thoughtlessness, by its insensitivity, the government has destroyed so much of the fabric that was Canada, the Canada so many of us knew and for whose survival so many of us were prepared to pay a high price. The government's insensitivity has eaten deeply into the fund of good will toward the French-speaking parts of our country which I can testify was alive and thriving. That fund of good will is now sadly depleted and dissipated. How it is to be restored is a question which causes me great concern.
I speak from personal experience. I know the good will which was there. It was in that climate of good will, and in the belief that national unity would be strengthened thereby, that French was made a compulsory subject in our high schools in British Columbia and, I believe, in other western provinces as well. Now that is gone; French is no longer compulsory. The good will is there and it fostered the creation of first-rate French language faculties in our western universities. Its presence explains the motivation of those who made the effort,
Commissioner of Official Languages long before recent governments invented such words as "bilingual", to learn and to use Canada's other language, thereby building increasingly effective links between the two major linguistic communities in this country.
There is an expression we use in English indicating that when circumstances warrant we are speaking more in sorrow than in anger. Today I speak in sorrow and in anger when I look at what the government has done to my country. [Translation]
Being a westerner, Mr. Speaker, and having made the effort to bring the two linguistic communities of my country closer, thanks to the facilities and good will which existed in the west,
I share those feelings. Consequently I condemn this government for having alienated my region from the remainder of Canada with a total lack of sensitivity for what Canada represents for westerners and for its serious political and social consequences.
In spite of various warnings from every quarter, including the annual warnings of the Commissioner of Official Languages, this government undertook without any misgiving to enforce a senseless and obsolete linguistic policy. That government policy has so seriously alienated western Canada that even some separatist movements are being set up there.
I particularly regret the confrontations the government has brought on and the cultural frictions it has caused with its stubborn and obstinate language policy.

I am deeply saddened, and I am angry. I am also fearful of what the future holds. The government has brought us to a sad pass. In 1967 there was virtually no separatism in Quebec. It was the year of the centennial, of jubilation. In 1968, only 10 per cent showed itself. By 1970 there were serious cracks in the national structure. By 1974 the separatist vote had risen to 24 per cent, and by 1976 to 40 per cent or more. A government is now in place in the province of Quebec dedicated to separatism and, what is more, veering ever more strongly toward unilingualism.
The government has failed the Canadian people through its inability to put across to the nation the worthy purposes of the Official Languages Act. It has driven the west further away from Ottawa, as well. There is a crying need today, as never before, to re-evaluate the programs, the practices and the instruments used to make the Official Languages Act acceptable across this land. Warnings as to this need have been placed before the government in the various reports presented by the languages commissioner and in many studies undertaken in this field, notably in the Bibeau report and, even more recently, in the Lamy report from the University of Ottawa. Does the government intend to allow an inquiry to be undertaken? My leader has suggested that there should be an. inquiry set up into the practices underlying the application of the bilingual program.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid time will not permit me to give you examples of texts used in schools for teaching the other

April 1, 1977
Commissioner of Official Languages official language. I have some here. I have submitted them to the attention of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and the Chairman of the Public Service Commission.
I feel that some of these texts are harmful. They are vindictive and malicious, they seek to destroy the notion of a Canada from sea to sea. They breed contempt among those who could otherwise live in harmony and as brothers.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, those texts and perhaps others could be discussed at the time of the inquiry my party is calling for, an inquiry that is truly necessary to examine closely the mistakes made by the government in setting up a language policy which, far from uniting this country, has seriously divided it.

There are other matters which such an inquiry could pursue; for example, the quality of the instruction and the attitude of the instructors as well as the value of sending public servants on language courses a year or so before they are due for retirement.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, once again I urge the government to allow Mr. Spicer's report to be referred to a parliamentary committee so it may initiate an inquiry into the government's language policy. In the meantime, in view of the commissioner's frankness and objectivity, we will not raise any objections to extending his term as proposed by the government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that we have, so close to a budget which has caused such great distress to both the business community and to the army of unemployed in Canada, consideration of a motion to adjourn the House, because this motion must be framed against the background of that budget. The budget was aptly described this morning by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) as a master plan for unemployment in Canada. There are now over 900,000 unemployed people in this country. There is disaster in the fishing industry, there are difficulties in the farming community and there are a whole host of other things the budget has failed to attack. Therefore, I think it interesting that we should be asked to adjourn the House at this time.
The 932,000 Canadians who are out of work do not include the hidden jobless of Canada. The seasonally adjusted rate is 7.9 per cent, but there are many people in this country who are being seasonally adjusted out of what is their birthright, namely, working and helping to develop this country. The Conference Board of Canada predicts 8.3 per cent unemployment for the fourth quarter of this year. The unemployment crisis which particularly affects young people in all parts of Canada, but especially in the five eastern provinces, ought not to be forgotten by this House as we consider a motion to leave this place.
Sixteen of every 100 young persons looking for work in this country are unable to find jobs. Eighty per cent of last year's unemployment was created in the five eastern provinces. Young people, who make up one fifth of our population,
April 1, 1977

comprise two-fifths of the unemployed. The five eastern provinces contain 34 per cent of the population but carry 45 per cent of the unemployed in Canada. The unemployment rate among the young is now nearly twice the average.
So is it any wonder that in some parts of this country there is disenchantment? Is it any wonder that young people in some parts of the country begin to look to other options to realize their own personal ambitions? Every member of this House would wish it otherwise, but this government must take a great deal of the responsibility for this situation which exists among our young people today, a situation that last night's budget goes nowhere to meet.
Another aspect which last night's budget fails to deal with is the present uncertainty in the business community. The private sector asked nothing of the government except the opportunity of knowing what are the government's intentions so that it can properly plan ahead. The fact is that since 1975 Canadians have been investing more abroad than foreign-owned corporations have been investing in Canada. This is a phenomenon the results of which we have not yet fully felt in this country. The situation is most alarming vis-a-vis the United States. There are direct foreign investment outflows to the United States to the extent of $556 million this year. In other words, Canadian business enterprise is looking elsewhere. Business enterprise is looking beyond the rhetoric of the government to the facts of the matter, and the facts show that in other countries it is easier to make one's way since there is more certainty in their business communities.
Is there any member of this House who could look at last night's budget and feel that it had moved in a direction that would provide hope either to the unemployed and their future or to business development, which is the best prospect for overcoming unemployment in Canada in a permanent way? I think the answer to that question must be known. The government is responsible for that, not parliament.
We had an example today of what I think is an irresponsible approach to the operation of this House. In face of an adjournment motion on the order paper, the New Democratic Party decided to thwart the legitimate operation of parliament by proposing an adjournment motion to cut off debate for this day.
Shame.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
In face of an adjournment motion on the order paper of the House which was there to be read by all who wanted to do so, the New Democratic Party used a parliamentary gimmick which would have cut off the right of the members of this House to deal with some very important legislation on that order paper. If that motion had carried, Bill C-2, the Advance Payments for Crops Act, would not have been dealt with. That is legislation which this party supports. I do not know if the government knew what would happen in the course of the debate in this House. Bill C-26 is sitting on the order paper. If reorganization of the scientific community in this country could have been reached, it could not have been reached today. This reorganization is something
Easter Recess
for which the university community is crying out. I am not excusing what I have commented on before, namely, the operation of this House of Commons and the kind of legislation that we have to deal with from time to time. There are circumstances when it would be equally wrong for me to commend and advocate support. The adjournment motion is already on the order paper of the House of Commons. I have described the motion put forward by the New Democratic Party as a parliamentary gimmick. The motion, by its very terms and in the context which I have spoken, would give some fuel to those who say that parliament has become irrelevant. I think the NDP ought to be ashamed of itself.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a point of order. I have sat patiently listening to the hon. member's little speech, but may I remind him that he has been violating Standing Order 35, which reads:
No member may reflect upon any vote of the House, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
That vote was taken this morning. It stands as a judgment of the House. What the hon. member was saying was completely out of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say that I was not commenting on the vote on the motion that was before the House. I was commenting on the motion put forward by the New Democratic Party. There is quite a difference, I would suggest. In any event, that is the situation. What should be done with this motion? Should it be allowed to pass? If so, why? I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all members of the House that this motion should be allowed to pass.
What a surprise.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is important that members of parliament who support the government, who day after day vote approval for programs, and who thumped loudly last night at a budget that was inadequate, be allowed to go home for a few days at Easter time to see their constituents.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

They will find out what their constituents think about that budget, that program and their supporters. It might be very enlightening for the NDP members as well. Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow the prince of sophistry when speaking in debate in this House. The House leader of the Tory party has just outdone himself in the incredible performance we have witnessed in the last few minutes. I will come to the government in a minute. We have the official opposition who witnessed the budget which I read in the lock-up yesterday and then heard it presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) last night. I could have sworn that it was written by the financial critic of the Tory party because it was so conservative. It was, however, a budget that the official opposition in Canada said was so harmful for the unemployed, was going to do nothing to produce jobs, was going to leave the Canadian economy basically as it has been and in a solid state of stagnation for the remainder of 1977. They were condemning the budget on one hand, but on the other hand they had to admit that the basic policies advocated by the government were taken from Conservative suggestions made in the past couple of months.
Then we had the performance this afternoon of the Conservative House leader when he had an opportunity of saying that the opposition in the House is against adjourning at this time until the government does something about unemployment. Instead, we get that master of sophistry saying, "No, we cannot vote against an adjournment motion because government members have to be allowed to get back to their constituents."

The members of the House of Commons do not need an adjournment for an extended week beyond that to find out what the people of Canada think of the budget. I have never heard such a phony argument as was presented this afternoon by the House leader of the Conservative party.
A point was raised about the motion I put forward on behalf of my colleagues this morning after the question period. The motion, if it had carried, would have adjourned the House for the day. So we would have been back here on Monday. If that motion had carried, we would not have debated during the three hours that will be put in this afternoon in the House of Commons. The reason the motion was moved today was that it was the first opportunity, under the rules of the House, for an opposition that really cares about unemployment in Canada to unite in showing Canada what it thinks of the government's disastrous budget.
If the Conservative party knew at least for an hour during any one period of the day where it stood on an issue, it would have said, "we do not like that budget. We think the government has failed glaringly to deal with the problems of unemployment, and we will vote to set aside the business of the House as a visible demonstration of our contempt for this government." Instead, I suspect, if I can put it bluntly, that because they did not think of moving the motion themselves, instead of wanting to have a united opposition showing their contempt for the government, they voted with the government despite the fact that their financial spokesman the night before went on television and radio across the country and said the government had brought in a budget that was disastrous for the country. When the opportunity came this morning to give a visible demonstration on behalf of the unemployed in Canada of what they thought of this government, instead of voting against it they voted with the government.
The government House leader has just said that such a motion was contemptuous of parliament. I remind the Conservative House leader that just about a year ago the Conservative party did support an NDP motion for adjournment of the House.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, the Conservative party, in one of those rare aberrations, knew for more than two hours where they stood on an issue and they happened to vote with us on a major matter then facing the country for an adjournment of the House, acknowledging that it was a symbolic gesture. We do not pretend it is anything other than that. It is a kind of visible expression at least of what members of parliament at a given time think of an extraordinarily bad performance by the government. That is why a year ago, at the time of the so-called judges' affair when the government was behaving in a contemptible fashion we did not hesitate to move adjournment. Similarly, the government, at a time when we have had the worst unemployment figures since the depression for six months in a row, brings in a budget which has as its basic assumption that unemployment will continue throughout 1977 at the same abysmal level. That is why we did not hesitate to bring forward a motion for adjournment today. We had hoped we would get the support of the official opposition. Instead, we saw them lining up solidly with the government.
Prior to the budget last night, the NDP was in fact prepared to support the motion for adjournment on condition that something would be brought down in the budget that would present tangible evidence that the government had come to its senses. For the last two months, day after day in the question period the government, in response to questions about what they are doing about unemployment, whether it is unemployment affecting the young, women, or family men, has consistently said, "Wait till you see the budget". We waited, and we saw it. We decided, after seeing the budget, that we cannot support an adjournment of the House at this time until the government brings forward some legislation that gives tangible proof that they have some concern about the unemployed in Canada.
What did we see in the document last night? We received the document which I think was ghost-written by a combination of R. B. Bennett and Herbert Hoover, so outmoded in its economic thinking and social commitment that even I was surprised to first read it and then hear it delivered in the House at a time when industry in almost every province across Canada has 20 per cent of unused capacity, which means that there is machinery and there are facilities in the plants that are not used. At a time when we have that excess capacity, what has the economic genius of the government come up with as a method of improving employment opportunities? What
Easter Recess
they came up with is another $1 billion hand-out to the corporate sector, a massive incentive program designed to cause the same factories to expand their plant facilities which are already underutilized.
I simply cannot understand the logic of the argument. Because we believe in a strong and healthy sector in the economy, my party supports a government economic program designed to stimulate economic growth and to increase the productivity of the private sector and designed at a time like this in our industry to provide grants or special tax concessions if they would lead to the important objective of employment for more people. But it is precisely because the government's approach at this time will lead to the opposite result that we want nothing to do with it. If the plant capacity were at 100 per cent, if the factories across the land were hard pressed in terms of their capacity to produce more goods and services at a time when we have one million unemployed, then some kind of stimulation to the private sector for expanding their capital capacity might make sense. But it makes absolutely no economic sense at this time to provide the $1 billion give-away that the government has given the corporate sector.
All that the $1 billion will do is give the corporations an unneeded increase in their profits during the coming fiscal year. At the same time, instead of recognizing that what we needed was an increase in demand, a demand for ordinary families to increase their consumption and following that through with providing a major stimulus by providing a major tax reduction, the government did just the opposite in terms of its tax reductions to the ordinary taxpayer in Canada. It could not be more economically foolish at a time when we are still experiencing high levels of inflation, and it is cruel to the ordinary taxpayers. The NDP has said that that is where the significant tax change should have taken place. We put forward the proposition that we needed a $500 million tax reduction which should go to middle and low income Canadians.
We would abolish the system of indexation. That should have been abolished in this budget. That would have netted for the treasury about $1 billion. In addition, there should have been an across-the-board tax reduction of $1.5 billion which would begin with the low income earner and tail off with the $25,000 a year earner. Everyone earning more than that would get nothing, and those earning less would get larger reductions in proportion to income. By abolishing the system of indexation and by providing that kind of tax reduction there could have been a net impact on the economy of some $500 million which would have stimulated, on the demand side of the economy, the production of goods and services, which would have resulted in calling back to work the one million men, women and young people who find themselves unemployed at this time. That is one step in the short run. In addition-

Mr. Speaker, I will not say what ought to be said more properly, as you have indicated, in a budget debate, but I will make some suggestions about the kind of legislation our party believes should be brought in before we adjourn. Putting this particular iniquitous budget to one side, I will emphasize in my comments from now on the things we think the government should bring in before the House recesses. Among these, as I have already said, there should be a new measure which would give a significant tax reduction to middle and low income people.
Second, we think there should be a bill introduced by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) which would lead to a major increase in the government's budget to allow for the building of more low-cost housing. There is no doubt that there is a glut in the market from coast to coast of homes which are in the $80,000 to $125,000 category. There is no doubt that well paid lawyers, doctors or members of parliament can find a large housing supply, but people who work in fish plants in St. John's, in a mine in Sudbury, where workers are reasonably well paid on a comparative basis for industrial workers, and farmers in the ordinary parts of Saskatchewan-not one of the affluent parts-can still not afford to buy a house or to rent a house at reasonable rent levels.
If the government wants to do something about unemployment before we adjourn, it should provide legislation which shows that the government believes in a major increase in the supply of low-cost housing. This would provide badly needed jobs and would provide a badly needed social requirement, namely, homes for people who need them.
In addition, we would like to see the government live up to the commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in July of 1974 to provide some $290 million in financial assistance to municipalities across Canada to introduce or expand urban transit facilities. That is needed now as a job creation measure, which would certainly benefit all the metropolitan regions across the country, and it would also benefit the country as a whole because it would lead ultimately to less consumption of badly needed energy.
We would like to see the government bring forward legislation which would do for all of Canada what has been done for Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, namely, provide a national program of insulation for Canadian homes.
Hear, hear!

I am glad to see a Liberal member applaud that point. I hope he will join in the debate. This program makes sense in Nova Scotia and in Prince Edward Island, and there is no reason why it would not make sense in the rest of the provinces. This kind of measure would immediately provide jobs in every town, village and city across the land, and it would reduce the consumption of energy in the winter months of next year.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
We would like to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) bring in a bill next week announcing a major expansion of public works projects across Canada. If he could just put back on to the record the legislation he set aside when the period of restraint was inaugurated a year and a half ago, it would be supported by this party, and it could pass through the House of Commons. Projects of that kind would provide jobs right across the land.
There are a number of short-run proposals we think the government should act upon before we adjourn. We think there should be a tax cut, that the housing industry should be stimulated, and that there should be more capital works projects and assistance for urban transportation. There is nothing remarkably profound or innovative about these proposals. Anybody in Canada who is concerned about employment and simultaneously concerned about economic responsibility could advocate these proposals. A concerned government would not only have advocated them, but would have put them into the budget last night.
My party fully recognizes that the proposals I have just made are short run. Even if they were all accepted by the government and carried out, they would not create by the end of 1977 or 1978 anything approaching full employment. It would be deceptive to suggest that that would be the case, but they would constitute a major beginning which we did not get in last night's budget.
Before we adjourn we would like to see the government bring in a bill committed to creating full employment over a period of years and to setting specific targets. Last fall on behalf of my party I proposed such a program. It was the result of about a year's work by a number of people in my party. I will not present all the details of the program today in the House. I have done that before, but this program stipulates that if we had a government which was committed to serious action, we could indeed have virtually full employment at the end of a four-year period. That is precisely what the people of Canada want to see. They do not expect miracles. They do not expect a government which is faced with one million unemployed to come up with a program which, within six months or a year, would make all our problems go away. However, the people expect the government to make a long range commitment which is backed up by specific proposals, for example, to move from the misery of the winter of 1977 to a winter of perhaps some contentment four years down the road.
My party would like to see the government bring in a full employment bill which would set out specific targets, and which would make it mandatory for the minister to report to the House at least once a year justifying his targets for that year and explaining how government has or has not lived up to its targets for the preceding year. In short, we would like to see the government commit itself to long range planning with regard to employment and with regard to the economic situation in general.
I said a moment ago that the people of Canada do not expect miracles. They do not expect politicians to have simple remedies to complex problems, but they do like to see a

government which recognizes the complexity of an issue, which recognizes the complexity of the nature of the Canadian economy, and which suggests how to get out of our current structural problems.
In addition to what I said about a full employment bill, my party also believes the government has to do something about the problem of economic independence in Canada. We believe that the problems of the Canadian economy are inextricably connected with the fact that the vast majority of our material resources are owned and controlled outside our borders. Of course we do not make villains of those investors, whether they live in the United States, Germany or any other country. That would be absurd because we have invited them into Canada.

With due respect, Mr. Speaker, I will try to follow your guidelines. I was outlining to the House the reasons why we oppose this motion. In general terms we believe that the government has done nothing about unemployment up to this point, and specifically that the budget last night gave no indication at all that it wants to deal with unemployment in the coming year.
If we get some action from the government along the lines I am suggesting, within the next few days or next week, then we would be prepared to support the motion for adjournment. I want to stress that the points I am making are germane to the motion, namely, whether or not we should be adjourning at the time the motion stipulates.
I should like to see the government commit itself to long-range changes in the structure of the Canadian economy. That is absolutely essential if we are to solve our balance of payments problem and the situation where we export our raw materials to other countries, something which creates labour intensive industries abroad instead of them being created in Canada. We know it is a difficult task to create an economy
Easter Recess
that can provide full employment. We also know that if the government would level with the people and show that, although it is a difficult task, it wants to take these important structural moves over a period of years in order to lead to more employment, the people would respect that and support it. It is the government's total lack of action on that kind of long-range planning that got us into our present difficulty and keeps us there.
Related to the point I made about planning for full employment and planning for a structural change in the Canadian economy, which is absolutely essential for full employment, there is a third requirement that I should like to put forward on behalf of my party. During the next week we feel that the government should give some visible testimony of its recognition that it must move from boom and bust politics. It deals with inflation during one 18-month period forgetting about unemployment, then shifts to unemployment for another 18 months and forgets about inflation. That has been the characteristic pattern of Liberal governments in Canada since World War II and it can be documented very easily. They are masters of ad hocery; they are the creators of the cyclical difficulties we got into in the national economy. What we need is a commitment to national planning that would entail, for example, substantial control over the allocation of investment.
Even a Liberal government would be able to acknowledge the achievements of Sweden, West Germany or Japan. With the exception of Japan, those countries have social democratic governments but they are all characterized by their commitment to national economic planning-a commitment to the view that the government of the day must play a leading role in establishing the investment pattern for the years ahead.
We propose that in Canada, within the Department of Finance or some other department, a special planning body should be established to administer a special tax such as that which has worked so well in Sweden. I am sure the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) knows about it and perhaps he would even support it, at least privately, in cabinet. A tax mechanism has been instituted in Sweden that is used to level out the boom and bust nature of a market economy. During a period of high inflation a special tax is levied on the largest corporations. The funds from this tax are kept separately and not used for general revenue purposes. When unemployment emerges in the economy the government channels these funds back to the private sector, to the firms it got the money from in the first place, and on an approved project basis it makes sure jobs are created when they are needed. That is what planning is all about.
Any time the government gets messing in things like that, watch out.

The hon. member says that when the government gets involved like that we had better look out. I suggest that of all countries in the western world coping with inflation and unemployment, Sweden is most successful.

I know it is always a burden for a Tory to listen to an idea that originated more recently than the 18th century, but I hope that if only by osmosis these ideas will work their way through.
I want to conclude by saying we are opposed to this motion for adjournment because we recognize the unemployment picture in our country is a human and economic tragedy. People want to work. They do not want handouts. They want a government that is committed to dealing with unemployment. They do not expect magical recipes. They want a government that believes in taking concrete action.
I was dismayed the other day to hear someone call out from the benches to my right that the people want to collect unemployment insurance. Mr. Speaker, ten days ago when I was in British Columbia one of the most moving experiences I had was in listening to a 59 year old woman describe what happened in the small town of Abbotsford when the McDonald hamburger chain announced it had about 20 positions open. These youths, who so many people in Canada seem to assume do not want to work and would be delighted to continue collecting unemployment insurance or welfare indefinitely, turned up for those jobs. Do you know how many turned up? For about 20 jobs at a McDonald's hamburg stand, there was a line-up of young people three blocks long. They turned up the night before with haversacks and sleeping bags because they wanted work. If the line-up was three blocks long, there must have been hundreds of them turned away.
How many were still in school?

The point is that the people of Canada, the young people in particular, want work and not handouts. They expect from their governments a commitment to provide jobs, if not for tomorrow at least for the end of the year. We got nothing of this kind from this government. What we got from this government was a budget that says that when December, 1977, comes, like December, 1976, we are going to have one million Canadians unemployed. Therefore the New Democratic Party will not support a motion for adjournment until the government gives some testimony during the next few days or weeks to the fact that it has recognized that unemployment is
(Mr. Broadbent.]
a national, economic, and human disgrace, and is prepared to do something about it.

He began the same as he ended, with the feeling that only they have a heart, only they feel for the youth, and only they feel for the unemployed. I am going to start where he left off.
The Leader of the NDP talked about the line-up looking for work at McDonald's in British Columbia. I did not happen to be there, but I have seen the same circumstance on many, many occasions. I remind him when he comes along with his sophistry and, above all, his hypocrisy, that they had a government in British Columbia-
A good one.
It sure was. It was headed by Mr. Barrett. They drove out investment, closed the mines and closed the resources.
Shame!
They do not like to hear the truth.
What is the unemployment level today?
Do you want to make a speech?
Yes.

Well, just have a little patience. Listen for a few moments. The hon. member shows respects in committee. I hope he will show it this afternoon because I am going to say some things that I know will hurt him.
That NDP government drove out business. When you drive out business as well as the development and the resource industry, you dry up jobs. That is one of the problems in British Columbia today. Every time they mention the Conservatives they go back to the nineteenth century, or whatever century they want to talk about. The socialists have not had a new idea since their program was first designed. They have been preaching the same stuff for 25 years. Wherever they preached it, either in British Columbia, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, unemployment grew.
Oh, oh!
What about Saskatchewan?
The hon. member talks about Saskatchewan. Let me ask this: what province has lost more people than the province of Saskatchewan under the NDP?
Hear, hear!

What about the Tory government in
Newfoundland?

We saw the hypocrisy this morning. The NDP moved a motion. They have been fighting for a 20 or 30 hour week to increase the cost of production in order to drive us out of world markets. This morning they moved a motion so that they could have this afternoon off. That is why they moved that motion.
Shame!

The NDP are against investment, whether it is foreign investment or Canadian corporations. They want to dry it up. I would remind them that when we went out of office in 1963, the budget of this country was $6 billion. That is what the deficit is today.
In 1972 we had a minority government. I recall the great marriage in those days. The Liberals could only stay in power with David Lewis. Hear, hear!
They applaud.
We don't interject.

If the NDP could grasp one point, it should be that jobs come from growth. He complained about the $6 billion deficit, the imbalance of trade and the imbalance of payments. they are sold throughout the world, can compete in the market. Without that, you will never get full employment.
