Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to follow my friend from Calgary North, my great and tranquil friend, and I would like to say to him that we have tried to present many new ideas in this House. Maybe I can respond a bit to some of the old ideas that he has presented.
First of all, he was talking in a tone that makes me think that he and his party are all of a sudden very afraid of the NDP. They spent the whole day talking about the NDP. I think they must sense a new public opinion poll coming and suddenly they are afraid of us rather than of the Liberal party. They are directing their attention to our party. That sounds very interesting. Perhaps they and their party are going down, and that very, very quickly. They must be afraid of all these new ideas that we have been presenting because the Canadian people see the Conservative party as getting further and further behind all the time.
The member from Calgary North suggested we might compare any NDP province with any other province. I want to do that just for one second because I come from the province of Saskatchewan. Let us have a look at Saskatchewan. I think we have a lot of prosperity in that province now, considering the ingredients that we have. We do not have all the black gold that Alberta has and all the billions and billions of dollars worth of oil. What we have in Saskatchewan has been put together through the shrewd planning of a good government over the last 20 years. As a result of that, we now have the lowest unemployment of any province in the country.
They leave, that's why. They leave because there is no work. How many thousands have left Saskatchewan in the last 20 years?

1 am glad to respond to the question asked by the hon. member for Calgary North. He talks about all the people leaving Saskatchewan since the NDP came in. We can show him statistics. When the old CCF party was defeated in Saskatchewan in 1964 we had a population of about 980,000. When Thatcher took over, perhaps the most conservative Liberal we have seen in this country, the population started to dwindle year after year. In 1971 or 1972 when the NDP government took power in Saskatchewan we were down to about 909,000 people.

If the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) were to read he would find now that the population of Saskatchewan is climbing back up toward the 1 million mark. We are back to close to 950,000 people because we have a good government and because of the planning that has gone on.
The other question the hon. member asked was this: he asked us to compare a province like Saskatchewan to provinces which have had free enterprise governments. I should like to compare it to Newfoundland. Newfoundland has a Tory government. I should like compare it to any of the Atlantic provinces. I should even like to compare it to the province of Quebec in terms of unemployment and the average standard of living. Those other provinces have had free enterprise government. I should like to compare it to the province of Ontario. Look at all the assets Ontario has, all the tariff protection it enjoys under the freight rate structure. And despite that, they have a higher unemployment rate than we do. They do not have in Ontario an education or health system any better than ours, working from assets that are a lot less than those of Ontario.
We depend, as the hon. member knows, upon a farm economy which is terribly vulnerable, depending on international prices, whereas Ontario has a stable economy based on a strong manufacturing sector. If only they had an NDP government in Ontario which would plan the economy, just think what living standards the people of Ontario would have with all those resources, and if you had an NDP government in Alberta, with all that black gold to use, to plan for the people of Alberta they would be so wealthy that even the hon. member for Calgary North would be embarrassed.
When the CCF took over in Saskatchewan, people did not have electricity. They were in poverty. This is what the hon. member fails to realize.
You would have had drilling rigs too, if you had not driven them out. You drove them right out of the province. Thousands and thousands of people have left Saskatchewan.

I want to come back to the hon. member for Calgary North when he said: if you are losing an argument, you start to shout. But I do not want to do that because I would embarrass him. Anyway, he said our party was not concerned about growth or productivity or making our goods competitive around the world. Yet these are some of the very premises of social democratic policy.
Our party has been calling for budgetary measures to stimulate consumer demand. We need more consumer demand, and the best way to get that is to give a tax cut to the low income people and to decrease sales taxes so that lower income people can buy more clothing, more food, more consumer goods generally, which in turn would stimulate the economy. These are things for which our party has asked time and time again. We will continue to do so until the hon. member for Calgary North understands what a social democratic party is all about.
April 1, 1977

I oppose the motion not just for that reason but also because the budget which was brought down is a real affront and insult to the million or more people who are unemployed. I cannot in good conscience leave parliament without at least trying to encourage the government across the way to bring down a bill-
Why don't you do something about it then?

We moved a motion today, Mr. Speaker, which is one of the few ways we can protest the budget which was terribly inequitable and cruel to over one millon unemployed workers. If the Tory party had supported our motion and it had gone through, perhaps the government could have spent the day planning new legislation to help some of the unemployed and put them back to work.
Our party is not like the Conservative party. The Conservative party would sooner have people drawing unemployment insurance benefits and collecting welfare than have the government come in with good, sound legislation to put Canadians back to work. We have never been a welfare party. We have always been a party which says that the Canadian people should work and make a contribution to society. The Conservative party members are willing to sit on their fannies and watch more than one million people remain unemployed. They are willing to have the ordinary worker see an increase in his UIC contributions to pay for the unemployed. That is the kind of taxation that they endorse. They are willing to see Canadian taxpayers pay more taxes to pay for bigger welfare bills.
Why don't you give us a few new ideas.

We are saying we should sit here during the recess and discuss legislation. We should cancel the recess. We should oppose the motion and sit here through the recess so as to bring in new legislation to put Canadians back to work.
There are a lot of things that could be done to put Canadians back to work. The government could bring in a housing bill. It has experts at work in the Department of Urban Affairs.
Houses are selling in Calgary.

But who are buying houses in Calgary? Are they being sold to the unemployed, to the ordinary worker, or to the old age pensioner? I do not think so. There is a surplus of housing for some in this country, those who have large incomes, not low or modest incomes. It is the latter I am concerned about. We could dispose of a housing bill very quickly. There is no quicker way to put people to work than to build houses for people of low income.
In addition, the government could bring in a capital works program so that hundreds of millions of dollars could be spent in municipalities to improve services. That would put people to work and give them a sense of purpose. This country is drifting, Mr. Speaker; surely to God we all recognize that. Yet
Easter Recess
the Conservative opposition is not prepared to say to the Liberal party: "Come before the House with new legislation".
There was one more reason why I have to oppose the motion to adjourn the House.
You sound like the last supper.

The hon. member says I sound like the last supper. Perhaps I am influenced by the member who spoke before me. I noticed recently that there has been a tremendous drop in farm incomes. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board are not bringing into the House any new ideas or legislation to stop this slide in farm incomes. They are not even here this afternoon.
StatsCan a couple of weeks ago came out with statistics which I think should shock each and every one of us. From January, 1976, to January, 1977, gross farm income in Canada dropped some 31 per cent. In the province of Saskatchewan there was a drop in farm income of some 38 per cent, as was the case across western Canada. Many members might say, "So what? Farm income has been very high." I think this is another reason why we should not adjourn the House. If farm incomes continue to drop, not only does it hurt the farmers and force more off the land, driving more of them into poverty and creating misery in rural communities; it also means more unemployment for Canadians living in big cities and in central Canada. I say that because there is no consumer of goods who spends as much money as the farmer when he is receiving an adequate income. When farmers do not have income to spend, thousands and thousands of jobs will cease to exist. I refer to jobs in the farm machinery industry, the automotive industry, in all kinds of factories, the steel and rubber industry, as well as the fertilizer industry.
With a little imagination the government could stop that. It should now come before the House with a new dairy policy, which was promised before the end of March. The end of March was yesterday but we are still waiting for a dairy policy. How can I in good conscience agree to adjourn the House for a 12 day recess when the government has not brought in its dairy policy? How can I in good conscience agree to adjourn the House when my cow-calf operators are suffering, when the price of livestock is going down, the price of hogs is going down, and more and more small farmers in my riding are having more and more difficulty? The Minister of Agriculture could do something about this.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board could show some leadership by bringing into effect an international grains agreement which I am sure all of us on this side of the House would be in favour of. If the government would give some leadership in these areas, we in this party would be willing to support the adjournment of the House for an Easter break. I am sure all MPs would unanimously agree.
The budget gave a tax break of $300 million to individuals, which averages about $100 per family. At the same time the big Santa Claus is able to find about $1 billion for corporations, despite the fact that those corporations are already

April 1, 1977
Easter Recess
operating at about 80 per cent capacity. How can we go back and face our constituents with this kind of neanderthal budget, when the government could do so many things to stimulate the economy, such as giving tax breaks to low income earners?
The government could introduce programs to put people in Newfoundland, for example, back to work. I am sure Newfoundlanders like all others would like to work. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, this can be done. But it needs sound, economic planning by a government which believes that to stimulate the economy you start at the bottom by giving people of low income a bigger tax break. People on low income barely live from day to day. They have barely sufficient to purchase nutritious food to feed their families and to send their children to school. If people of low income were given an extra $200 or $500, they would spend that money, which in turn would stimulate the economy and, as the hon. member for Calgary North said, create more jobs. That is the way you do it. You do not do it by giving the oil companies, and the manufacturing companies a few more tax loopholes at the top when there is no guarantee they will spend that extra money on creating jobs for ordinary Canadians.
I cannot vote for the motion. I think it is an affront to the unemployed. I think it is an affront to have this government budget for a million unemployed.
Do you want to take a holiday today?

It is an affront tq the ordinary person. This country is going to have to pay for those unemployed. The Conservative party, the party of welfare, the party of unemployment, the party of dole, or the party that wants that kind of system can do it if it wishes. Our party believes that all Canadians should be given an opportunity to build up their country and make it a great country.
You spent $10,000 of the taxpayers' money foolishly by having a vote today.

If we had an opposition on this side of the House who were as concerned about this country, where it is going and its people, as the small group in our party, we could do it. It is only going to be done if we have a government with imagination bringing in many of the programs that our party has talked about time and time again. If we do that, we will put this country back to work and make it a better place in which to live for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. gentleman when he talked about how he would find it difficult in his conscience to vote for the motion which calls for the adjournment of the House over the Easter recess. I listened to him repeat that statement. Perhaps he can explain to me and to the House how he reconciles that statement with the motion of his leader at twelve o'clock, for which he voted. How can he say, in all conscience, that he is against the adjournment of the House?

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member who asked the question had more respect for parliament and had been here when I was speaking, he would not have asked that question. That is how I started off my speech.
He did not understand you because you speak in so many circles and never come to the point.

I am very glad to repeat it. I know that many Conservatives have very dense heads, but I did not think they were quite that bad. We did that this morning for two reasons. First, it was one of the only devices we had to protest the worst budget this country has ever had. We felt we had to make that protest at the earliest possible opportunity.
And waste parliamentary time?

By making that type of gesture, which some would call symbolic, this House would have adjourned for only two and a half or three hours. Perhaps during that time there could have been a cabinet meeting where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues could have gone back to the drawing board and brought forth some policies that would do something for the unemployed.
I know it is very difficult for the Liberals to be serious. Surely we can ask them that on behalf of the Canadian people. I thought the Conservative party would be interested in giving our Liberal friends an opportunity to do some more thinking. The government House leader said a few days ago that the Liberals in Toronto did some thinking, probably for the first time in 17 years. I was just hoping that we would be able to use a few hours this afternoon. With all the momentum they have going in terms of new ideas, perhaps they will come up with some new ideas for the unemployed. That is why I moved the motion today. That did not work, obviously. We did not have the support for that. We are saying now that we are against the motion to adjourn and want to force the government to come back into the House with some new ideas to put Canada back to work again. If the Conservatives do not like that, I cannot help it.

I hope he is more brilliant than his predecessor.

Mr. Speaker, I will try. I do not want to spend too much time on the by-play between the opposition parties in the House. It is, after all, only five minutes to four o'clock. To spend a lot of time dealing with the sort of criticism each of us is giving the other is not worth while since the Conservative party is becoming less and less relevant in the debate concerning this particular budget. If one examines the reaction of the Conservative critic in this matter, one will see that there are a lot of secret admirers in the official opposition for this particular budgetary paper that we are now considering.
My good friend from Calgary North had a few disparaging remarks to make about the previous government of the prov-
April 1, 1977

ince of British Columbia. I know he is an expert on the province of Alberta. Far be it from me ever to go to the province of Alberta and try to tell him anything about Alberta politics. In terms of the province of British Columbia, at the present time with its Social Credit-Conservative coalition government, unemployment is at an all-time high. It has never been worse. I want to tell the hon. member for Calgary North that business has never been unhappier than it is today in the province of British Columbia, and investment is lower in that province than it was under the New Democratic government that was recently turned out of office. The business community are thinking very hard about the decision they took in regard to that particular coalition.
As I say, I do not want to take a lot of time dealing with the by-play between this party and the official opposition because that is not what we are here to debate today. We are talking about whether this adjournment motion should be passed by the House. Every member in this House wants a holiday. We would all like to have a break. It is just a question of how high you put this rotten budget in your priorities, in the sense of where you should be spending your time as a member of parliament. This House should be in session until the government has taken another look. It can present new bills on Monday. It is not a problem in terms of rethinking some meaningful legislation.
What is most appalling in the budget is the political cynicism that is inherent in it. There is no question that the things the government has done today are going to be reversed exactly one year from now. It has deliberately decided to keep a million people unemployed because it does not want an election this year. That is the effect of this particular budget. What is going to happen is that in March of 1978 we will see an increase in corporate taxes; we will see substantial personal tax cuts at the lower level; and we will see a major capital works program.
Right on.

The cynicism is that that will be the election budget and it will be fought on the backs of the million unemployed in Canada. That is what will happen as far as this particular budget is concerned. The government has made a deliberate and callous political decision. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH COMMISSION OF INQUIRY TO INVESTIGATE ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-220, to provide for the constitution of a federal transport commission of inquiry (impartial investigation of transport accidents), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the seventh time in the last four or Five years that I brought this matter to the attention of this Chamber. I introduced it first on October 20, 1970 as Bill C-66. It has been in front of the House as that bill, as Bill C-85, Bill C-333, Bill C-109, Bill C-226, and now Bill C-220.
The subject matter of this bill wears well and it is high time the government took the initiative to resolve the principle at stake here, that is, the removal from the investigation of accidents in Canada of every trace of possible conflict of interest. I have a few general remarks to make and I will not be long. As the Chair is aware, we want to deal with this motion fairly shortly, but there are a couple of points I want to
4582

April 1, 1977
Transport Commission of Inquiry
make so that members of the House will be aware of the seriousness with which I approach this matter.
I suggest to my colleagues that they think for a moment of the tragedy which happened in the Canary Islands a few days ago. I ask them to reflect upon the conflict that may arise in the evidence and testimony, in the defence postures, the misleading information, and so on, in the attempt to identify the cause of that tragic runway collision between two jumbo jets. I ask members of the House to think where Canada would stand had that accident occurred at Dorval, Mirabel, Toronto, Vancouver or Halifax. What would the world think if they knew that Canada did not have an independent commission, removed from any possible conflict of interest, to investigate this matter? Let me give the background with respect to this.
No branch of the Department of Transport or other federal agency has over-all responsibility for ensuring that a systematic, comprehensive, and high standard of accident investigation is established and maintained in transportation sectors under federal jurisdiction. Instead, each transportation sector has a separate investigatory body attached to it. The aviation safety investigation division deals with air related accidents. The casualty investigations branch is responsible for marine accidents. The accident and defect investigations branch deals with land vehicles, trucks, buses, and interprovincial carriage. These are all independent, separate bodies, but they are also part of the Department of Transport, or Transport Canada as we call it now. Rail accidents are investigated by the rail safety and standards branch of the railway transport committee. Breaks in federally regulated pipelines are investigated on an ad hoc basis by the engineering branch of the National Energy Board.
Ordinarily, serious accidents which occur to aircraft, ships and vehicles used by the Crown in right of Canada would be investigated, or not as the case might be, by the above authorities. One exception, of course, has to do with accidents to military transport, and these will not be investigated by the above authorities unless a civilian vehicle, aircraft, or other mode of transport is involved in the accident. The point I am trying to make here is that we have a multiplicity of investigatory teams working for the same authority that is responsible for the regulatory aspects of the legislation.
For several years not only I but other members of the opposition, and people in the private sector, have been pressuring the government to establish an independent, and particularly an impartial, commission to investigate transportation accidents which fall under federal jurisdiction. That pressure has apparently had some influence. The Speech from the Throne of September 30, 1974, referred to the establishment of an independent accident investigation board as one of the new transportation initiatives. The government of that day was prepared to undertake-and I might add, undertake immediately, in their own words-the establishment of that board. When questioned in the House about the progress of such legislation, the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of transport advised the House that the government proposal was based on a study done by General A. MacLean who had studied existing federal organizations for the investigation of
[Mr. Forrestall.)
transportation accidents and the promotion of transportation safety.
In May of 1975 the then minister of transport assured the House that his department was "exercising pressure on the government House leader to bring in legislation as soon as possible". It was suggested at the time that legislation was in fact prepared. If such was the case and for some reason the government decided not to proceed, I would personally find that to be a matter of some regret. However, late in October of 1975 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), who had just assumed his responsibilities, said in response to a question in the House that the work on the legislation was "going forward".
Again in December he assured the House that he had every intention of introducing it. Mind you, he did not give us any specific date. He did suggest at the time that the subject matter of government legislation would be somewhat broader in scope than what was proposed by me in Bill C-220. Apart from extending the authority and responsibility of such an independent board to areas of provincial jurisdiction, I find it difficult to understand, for example, how it could have been much broader than mine because I covered everything that moves under federal or provincial jurisdiction. But I welcome the broadening of the act under provincial jurisdiction and the broadening of my bill to permit consultation with equivalent foreign authorities in pursuit of their investigative work. Perhaps authority could be given to name commissioners from time to conduct public inquiries of high concern such as, for example, the tragic accident in Tenerife a week ago. The point is that whatever he intended to do in 1975, he has not done much about it. This is something we regret.
During the December 2, 1976, meeting of the standing committee we again came back to this area. The standing committee had in front of it the deputy minister, Mr. Cloutier, of the Department of Transport, who said that the matter of an independent accident investigation board was still "under study within the department" and that a memorandum to the cabinet should be ready within six to eight weeks, in other words, by the end of January, 1977. I hope that that memorandum is in front of the cabinet. In his testimony Mr. Cloutier gave a hint as to why, despite the lapse of two years, neither the Department of Transport nor the government has evolved a firm and detailed policy. It might be useful if I read his testimony:
There are several alternatives possible. On the one side the present arrangements could be continued with an independent board which would, in effect, monitor, review and assess the work of the accident investigators that exist now, and that such a board could be given powers overall the loans.
That is how it appeared in the published report of the committee proceedings. The word should have been staff. It goes on to read:
Indeed we have already set up within the air administration such a board to which accident reports would be referred to. That is viewed as a temporary mechanism, if you wish, until the larger question is examined and decided upon. But the concept of such, if you wish, after-the-fact board is an alternative.
April 1, 1977

At the other end of the spectrum you could have a totally independent board-
That, incidentally, is what I am recommending.
-which would, in effect, absorb the investigators that exist in various agencies. This would have, in my view, some disadvantages. It would have certainly the advantage of removing any possible claim of conflict of interest, and that basically is at the root of the desirability of setting up such a board ...
There are some alternatives in between.
There are alternatives and mixes in between those two particular extremes. However, what concerns me is that nothing has happened. There are indications that one reason a decision has not been forthcoming is that the department has been internally divided on these alternatives. Generally speaking, opposition to a fully independent and separate accident investigation organization does not seem to be substantial at the departmental level, which is responsible for conducting accident investigations. Rather, this level seems wary of the proposal to establish some form of accident review board which, while not guaranteeing investigators complete independence from the department as a whole, would sit, as it were, in judgment on the work and on the reports of the department.
I go back to Mr. Cloutier in December of 1976 when he spoke in the committee. He referred to one drawback of a fully independent accident investigation board and said the following:
On the other hand it would have the disadvantage of removing from the inspection and certification specialists a concern, and I mean concern both in the intellectual as well as emotional and professional contexts-a concern for safety-that I think is of great value in the operating of a certification mechanism.
From the regulatory and enforcement standpoint such a board would have a number of other disadvantages; I recognize that myself. It might, for example, be more harsh and public in its criticisms of the regulatory and enforcement policies of the department as they pertain to the causes, direct and indirect, of accidents, and more persistent and demanding in pressing for changes related to safety.
I recognize that there are people who see in that a disadvantage to a fully independent board, but that is what we are here for. That is the purpose of this legislation. It is to remove once and for all any question of conflict in these very important matters. I am not blaming the department alone-as what I have been saying might indicate-for the excessive delay in developing proposals for a new accident investigation organization, although that is the exclusive responsibility of the department. There are a number of outside agencies and factors involved. Interdepartmental committees have difficulty ferreting out and establishing relationships between departments as they would relate to such an independent board. On the other hand, this matter has been before them for over three years now. I have been bringing this to the attention of hon. members since the winter of 1967-68.
This matter has been in bill form on five or six occasions. There has been agreement among the successive ministers of transport that there is a need in this country for such an independent board. There are indications from hon. members
Transport Commission of Inquiry on the government side that the cabinet approves of this idea, its concept and its principle. We understand from evidence given to us that documentation has been prepared, and possibly that draft legislation is part of the present scope of things.
If this is true, I am pleased. I hope somebody from the government side can fill us in with respect to that legislation so that we might move this bill to the committee stage, which I would prefer, or at least its subject matter, so that if the department needs further guidance it can come from witnesses who could be brought before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. If we could get the bill to that point, those witnesses would cover the industry in all aspects. They would cover pipelines, rail, air, interprovincial busing, marine movement, and the total scope of it.
I commend the principle of this bill to those who are concerned about transportation safety and about conflict of interest which arises when the regulatory body and the investigative body have the same bosses. We all saw the rush of officials of KLM to protect one of their own. I suggest that this in fact happens because that is human nature. Over the past six, seven or eight years I have cited a number of instances where there were clear conflicts and where the department, in my judgment, was at fault. Those reports and those investigations have not yet been completed. One of them is four or five years old. They will not be brought to a conclusion because the moment that is done there will be an admission of error, and friends will be responsible for the not very attractive fate of other friends. That is not good enough for a country such as Canada. It is not good enough in an age in which travel is as sophisticated as we all know it to be. We need a truly independent body which would have a priori right.
I will close my remarks this afternoon by briefly going through the explanatory note which accompanies the bill. The explanatory note reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to establish a permanent and impartial commission of inquiry to investigate transport accidents that are within federal jurisdiction. Under present laws, many of these transport accidents-perhaps resulting in loss of life-are investigated by the federal body that is responsible for making and enforcing the rules under which the transport operated when the accident occurred. There is an obvious conflict of interest in such case.
The commission hereby proposed would have exclusive, but selective, authority-as against any other federal body-to investigate all accidents resulting in death, injury, or property loss occurring on any transport under federal authority. However, the commission need not exercise this authority where it felt the public interest would be sufficiently served through an investigation by the appropriate federal regulatory body; that is, where the federal body would not be impeded by a conflict of interest in its investigations.
The commission would also have authority to investigate safety standards and practices and to recommend changes.
The commission would report its findings and recommendations, if any, to parliament to provide opportunity for public debate.
Provision is also made for any person whose conduct or judgment becomes an issue during the investigation to appear and be heard; and, in the event of his death or other disability, to have his interests represented by a person appointed by the commission.
I commend the subject matter of this bill to the thinking of hon. members. I suggest that in 1977 it is time we remove any appearance of conflict of interest from the conduct of the investigation of accidents.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH COMMISSION OF INQUIRY TO INVESTIGATE ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and his parliamentary secretary I have been asked to act in their names.
At the outset I wish to thank the hon. member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) for his patience and co-operation with us in dealing with this bill concerning the creation of an organization for impartial investigation of transport accidents. He must be setting a parliamentary record of sorts as this is, I believe, the sixth time the bill has been considered at private members' hour. However, unlike many other bills that are presented, the objective of this bill does command broad support from all parties, and we wish it to receive further consideration.
The government has spent a great deal of time over the past few years attempting to devise a structure which would have sufficient powers to deal effectively with accident investigations in the transportation field and yet be free of any charge of conflict of interests with existing regulatory and investigative bodies. Considerable progress has been achieved and it is expected that a recommendation to cabinet will be submitted within a matter of weeks.
The hon. member is aware as well that the government has reservations concerning some of the details of Bill C-220. One important area is the scope of activities of a commission and, of course, the funding provisions.
It is the government's intention to introduce shortly a comprehensive bill on this subject matter. I think the hon. member
for Dartmouth-Halifax East will feel some measure of satisfaction when this occurs.
In view of the circumstances, I wish to thank the hon. member for agreeing to withdraw his bill on the understanding that its subject matter be referred to the standing committee for further consideration.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis):
That all the words after the word "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor: Bill C-220, an act to provide for the constitution of a Federal Transport Commission of Inquiry (impartial investigation of transport accidents), be not now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the bill withdrawn and that the subject-matter thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
